conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I fell off my chair at home. I twisted my ankle and heard a pop. It hurt right away and swelled up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you feel dizzy or pass out before the fall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t. It was just a mechanical fall. I was trying to get up and lost my balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The X-ray shows a fracture in your lower tibia, but the ankle joint looks intact. No surgery is needed, but you’ll need to keep it immobilized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need surgery? That’s good. But walking is out of the question, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll be on crutches or a walker. We’ll arrange physical therapy and possibly rehab to help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t know about rehab. I just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but with your medical history, we want to make sure you’re safe. We also noticed something else—your INR was very high, at 7.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: INR? That’s from my Coumadin, right? I’ve been on it for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A normal INR is around 2 to 3 for someone on Coumadin. Yours was dangerously high, which increases bleeding risk. We’ve held the Coumadin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Should I be worried about bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. No signs of bleeding now. We’ll restart Coumadin at a lower dose once your INR comes down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You also mentioned shortness of breath when lying flat. Is that new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s been going on for a while. I think my legs are more swollen than usual too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows signs of fluid buildup, likely from your heart failure. We’ll give you some diuretics to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on Lasix. Is that not enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were on 40 mg twice daily. We’ll keep that for now and monitor your weight and symptoms. We want to see if you can lose some fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been having headaches too. Can I take my Imitrex?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can take it as prescribed. We’ll keep an eye on it. Also, I see you’re on methadone and Dilaudid for pain. Are you taking them regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Methadone three times a day, and Dilaudid when the pain gets bad. It’s been okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that regimen. Just let us know if you feel too drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did another chest X-ray. The heart looks a bit bigger, and there’s some fluid in the lungs. This confirms your heart failure is flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. We’ll continue the diuretics. You’ve already lost a few pounds—your weight dropped from 424 to 418. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t even notice. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked for pneumonia, but the consolidation in your lung base isn’t worsening. We don’t think antibiotics are needed yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been coughing a little, but not too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. One more thing—psychiatry spoke with you yesterday. Can we talk about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I said some things. I’ve been feeling really down. Unsafe at home. It’s been hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. They mentioned you’ve had trauma in the past?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I was raped ten months ago. I haven’t told many people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for sharing that. It takes courage. Psychiatry recommends starting Effexor for depression and anxiety. Would you be open to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess so. I need to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start it today. And we’ll connect you with a therapist after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is coming down—it’s now 2.9. We’re restarting Coumadin at 10 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that less than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were on 11–12 mg alternating. We’re starting lower to avoid another high INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Weight is now 410 lbs. Breathing easier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a bit. I can lie flatter now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to reduce your Lasix to once daily. If swelling or shortness of breath returns, go back to twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a rib X-ray because of your chest pain. No fracture. It’s likely musculoskeletal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts when I press on it. So not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look like a heart issue. We’ll keep managing it with your pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.4 on 11 mg daily. That’s in the safe range. The rehab facility will manage your Coumadin after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m going to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to help with mobility and recovery. You’ll continue physical therapy and get support for your mental health too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m a little nervous, but I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s labs look good. Your kidney function is stable, and your hemoglobin is normal. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my HIV and hepatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both are stable. You stayed on your HIV meds, and your liver enzymes are okay. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared for discharge. You’ll go to rehab, where they’ll help with your fracture recovery and continue your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated them: Coumadin is now 11 mg daily, Dilaudid is 4 mg every 6 hours as needed, and you’re starting Effexor 150 mg daily. All other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll follow up with my doctors after rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your PCP for blood pressure and INR, and a therapist for mental health. You’re doing great. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.
